title: Jeremiah 16:14–21
context: The LORD continues speaking. Suddenly he promises a new exodus: people will swear by the LORD who brought Israel back from the north and from all the lands of exile. Verses 14–15 closely resemble 23:7–8. The LORD then speaks of sending fishermen and hunters to search out the people, because their iniquity is not hidden from him. Jeremiah responds with a short prayer of confidence in the LORD as his strength and refuge, foreseeing the nations coming to confess that their idols are lies. The LORD answers that he will make them know his hand, his might, and his name.

verses.text: “Therefore behold, the days come,” says the LORD, “that it will no more be said, ‘As the LORD lives, who brought up the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt;’
verses.arminianNotes: "Therefore behold, the days come," says the LORD. Arminian readers see a sudden turn to hope. The exodus from Egypt will be eclipsed by a future act of deliverance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that this promise appears almost word for word in Jeremiah 23:7–8. They read the hope as rooted in God's faithfulness to his covenant even in the midst of judgment.

verses.text: but, ‘As the LORD lives, who brought up the children of Israel from the land of the north, and from all the countries where he had driven them.’ I will bring them again into their land that I gave to their fathers.
verses.arminianNotes: People will swear, "As the LORD lives, who brought up the children of Israel from the land of the north." Arminian readers see the LORD promising to bring the scattered people "again into their land that I gave to their fathers."
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the wording here differs slightly from 23:8, which speaks of "the offspring of the house of Israel." They name the difference without merging the passages. Both promise return from exile.

verses.text: “Behold, I will send for many fishermen,” says the LORD, “and they will fish them up. Afterward I will send for many hunters, and they will hunt them from every mountain, from every hill, and out of the clefts of the rocks.
verses.arminianNotes: "Behold, I will send for many fishermen." Arminian readers note that, in context, the fishermen and hunters seem to search out the people for judgment, since verse 17 says nothing is hidden. Some readers instead link the image to the gathering of verse 15.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same uncertainty and read the image mainly as judgment, given verses 17–18. The later image of "fishers for men" (Matthew 4:19) is sometimes compared, though its setting differs.

verses.text: For my eyes are on all their ways. They are not hidden from my face. Their iniquity isn’t concealed from my eyes.
verses.arminianNotes: "For my eyes are on all their ways." Arminian readers see that no one can escape the LORD's sight: "They are not hidden from my face." People are accountable for every hidden sin.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers compare Hebrews 4:13: "There is no creature that is hidden from his sight." The LORD's knowledge of every way is complete. Both traditions treat this as shared ground.

verses.text: First I will recompense their iniquity and their sin double, because they have polluted my land with the carcasses of their detestable things, and have filled my inheritance with their abominations.”
verses.arminianNotes: "First I will recompense their iniquity and their sin double." Arminian readers see judgment proportioned to the people's pollution of the land with "the carcasses of their detestable things."
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that "double" probably expresses full or complete payment rather than a precise mathematical measure. The land is the LORD's "inheritance," and its defilement is an offense against him.

verses.text: LORD, my strength, my stronghold, and my refuge in the day of affliction, the nations will come to you from the ends of the earth, and will say, “Our fathers have inherited nothing but lies, vanity and things in which there is no profit.
verses.arminianNotes: "LORD, my strength, my stronghold, and my refuge in the day of affliction." Arminian readers note that Jeremiah himself now speaks in prayer. He foresees the nations coming to confess that their fathers "inherited nothing but lies."
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in Jeremiah's prayer a hope for the nations, who will come "from the ends of the earth." They compare Isaiah 2:2, where "all nations shall flow" to the LORD's house.

verses.text: Should a man make to himself gods which yet are no gods?”
verses.arminianNotes: "Should a man make to himself gods which yet are no gods?" Arminian readers see the nations' own confession exposing the folly of idolatry. People make gods that cannot save them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that this is the confession the nations are pictured making in Jeremiah's prayer. Both traditions agree that idols are "no gods" and that trust in them is empty.

verses.text: “Therefore behold, I will cause them to know, this once I will cause them to know my hand and my might. Then they will know that my name is the LORD.”
verses.arminianNotes: "Therefore behold, I will cause them to know." Arminian readers see the LORD answering with a promise to make his power known, so that people will recognize "that my name is the LORD."
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the LORD himself causes people to know him, "this once." His hand and might reveal his name. Both traditions see the LORD making himself known as shared ground.
